3º de Primaria · Inglés

Have got / has got

Ficha para imprimir
123456
1

Pregunta de arranquePiensa 30 segundos antes de seguir

Tu amigo dice «I've got a dog» y su hermana dice «She's got a cat». ¿Por qué una vez es «have» y otra «has»?

Escribe o di en voz alta tu respuesta. Después .

Porque have got se usa con I, you, we, they, y has got con he, she, it (él, ella, ello). Las dos formas significan «tener». En las frases cortas se juntan: I've got, she's got.

2

Aprende15 apartados

Para empezar: The lost dog

Sam is very sad. His dog, Biscuit, is lost. Sam and his sister Mia make a poster to find him.

LOST DOG! Have you seen Biscuit? He's small and very friendly. He's got short brown fur and a white spot on his back. He's got long floppy ears and a short tail. He's got big black eyes and a pink nose. He hasn't got a collar, but he's got a red scarf around his neck. If you find him, please call Sam.

They put the poster on the trees in the park and on the door of the supermarket.

The next morning, Mrs Brown from number 12 knocks at the door. She's got grey hair and glasses, and she's got a basket in her hands.

"Hello, Sam. Have you got a small brown dog with a red scarf?" she asks.

"Yes, I have!" says Sam.

Mrs Brown opens the basket. Biscuit jumps out and licks Sam's face.

"Thank you, Mrs Brown!" says Sam.

"Thank you for your poster," she smiles. "Your description was perfect!"

1. What does have got mean?

We use have got to say what we have: things («I've got a new bike»), family and pets («I've got two cats») and parts of our body or appearance («I've got brown eyes»).

En castellano: have got significa «tener». Ojo: no sirve para la edad. En español «tengo ocho años», pero en inglés es «I am eight». Tampoco se usa para el hambre o el frío: «I'm hungry», «I'm cold».

2. Have got or has got?

The verb changes with the person. With I, you, we, they we use have got: «I have got», «They have got». With he, she, it we use has got: «He has got», «My sister has got», «The dog has got».

In speaking we use short forms: I've got, you've got, we've got, they've got; he's got, she's got, it's got. Truco: si puedes cambiar el sujeto por he, she o it, usa has: «Pablo (he) has got a ball».

3. Short forms: I've got, she's got

When we speak, and in informal writing, we usually use short forms (formas cortas). We join the subject and the verb with an apostrophe ('):

  • I have got → I've got
  • you have got → you've got
  • he has got → he's got
  • she has got → she's got
  • it has got → it's got
  • we have got → we've got
  • they have got → they've got

And in the negative:

  • have not → haven't: «I haven't got a bike.»
  • has not → hasn't: «She hasn't got a cat.»

Be careful! He's can mean two things:

  • «He's got a dog» = he has got.
  • «He's eight» = he is eight.

How do you know? Look for the word got. If got is there, 's means has.

Activity: rewrite these sentences with short forms: «We have got a garden. She has got long hair. They have not got a car.»

4. The negative: haven't got, hasn't got

To say that you do not have something, add not: haven't got (have not got) and hasn't got (has not got). «I haven't got a sister.» «My cat hasn't got a long tail.»

We often join a positive and a negative sentence with but: «I've got a brother, but I haven't got a sister.» «She's got a scooter, but she hasn't got a bike.» En castellano: en español basta con «no tengo»; en inglés el not va pegado a have o has.

5. Questions: Have you got…?

To ask, put Have or Has at the beginning: «Have you got a pet?», «Has your dad got a car?», «Have they got a garden?». Got stays in the middle.

Short answers repeat have or has, without got: «Yes, I have.» / «No, I haven't.» «Yes, he has.» / «No, he hasn't.» Ojo: no contestes «Yes, I have got»: es demasiado largo y suena raro.

6. A, an or any?

With have got we often use a, an or any before the noun:

  • a + one thing that starts with a consonant sound: «I've got a bike.»
  • an + one thing that starts with a vowel sound: «She's got an umbrella.» «I've got an orange.»
  • a number or some for more than one: «I've got two cats.» «We've got some books.»

In questions and negatives with plurals, we use any:

  • «Have you got any pets?» (¿Tienes mascotas?)
  • «I haven't got any brothers.» (No tengo hermanos.)
  • «Has she got any sweets?»

In Spanish we often say No tengo hermanos, without any word before the noun. In English, we need any: «I haven't got any brothers».

With one thing in negatives and questions, we use a or an: «I haven't got a dog.» «Have you got an eraser?»

Activity: ask a partner five questions with «Have you got any…?»: pets, cousins, brothers, posters, books.

7. Describing people: hair and eyes

We use have got to describe people. Hair can be long or short, straight (liso), curly (rizado) or wavy (ondulado), and blond (rubio), brown (castaño), black, red (pelirrojo) or grey. Eyes can be blue, green, brown or black.

«She's got long curly red hair and green eyes.» Ojo al orden: en inglés el adjetivo va delante: «long hair», no «hair long». Y hair no lleva -s: «He's got short hair».

8. Tall or short? Glasses and freckles

To describe people, we use be for size and shape, and have got for things on their body:

With be:

  • «She's tall.» (alta) / «He's short.» (bajo)
  • «He's thin.» (delgado) / «She's strong.» (fuerte)
  • «My grandpa is old.» / «My cousin is young.»

With have got:

  • glasses (gafas): «Mrs Brown has got glasses.»
  • freckles (pecas): «The twins have got freckles.»
  • a beard (barba) and a moustache (bigote): «My uncle has got a black beard.»
  • a fringe (flequillo), a ponytail (coleta), plaits (trenzas).

Remember the order of adjectives: size first, then colour: «She's got long brown hair.» Not brown long hair.

And remember: hair is singular in English. «Her hair is long» (not are). Never say hairs for the hair on your head.

To ask: «What does she look like?» (¿Cómo es físicamente?) – «She's tall and she's got curly hair.»

Activity: describe a person in your family with three sentences with be and three with have got.

Vídeo: What Does He Look Like? Song | Describing People · English Tree (YouTube) · 1,8 millones de visualizaciones

9. Body parts

To describe animals and monsters, we need the parts of the body: head (cabeza), eyes (ojos), ears (orejas), nose (nariz), mouth (boca), teeth (dientes), arms (brazos), hands (manos), legs (piernas), feet (pies) and, for animals, tail (cola), wings (alas) and fur (pelo de animal).

Plurales especiales: one foot → two feet; one tooth → many teeth. «An elephant has got big ears and a long nose (trunk).»

Vídeo: Head, Shoulders, Knees & Toes - Exercise Song For Kids · ChuChu TV Nursery Rhymes & Kids Songs (YouTube) · 1387,4 millones de visualizaciones

10. Animal bodies

Animals have got some body parts that people haven't got. Learn their names:

  • tail (cola): «A monkey has got a long tail.»
  • wings (alas): «Birds and butterflies have got wings.»
  • fur (pelaje): «A bear has got thick fur.»
  • feathers (plumas): «A parrot has got colourful feathers.»
  • beak (pico): «An eagle has got a strong beak.»
  • paws (patas con almohadillas) and claws (garras): «A cat has got soft paws and sharp claws.»
  • horns (cuernos): «A goat has got two horns.»
  • scales (escamas) and fins (aletas): «A fish has got scales and fins.»
  • a trunk (trompa): «An elephant has got a long trunk.»

To talk about one animal, we use it and has got: «It's got four legs and a tail.»

To talk about a group of animals, we use they and have got: «Elephants have got big ears.»

Animal riddles are fun: «It's grey. It's got big ears and a long trunk. What is it?» – «It's an elephant!»

Activity: write a riddle about your favourite animal with three sentences with has got.

11. Meet the monsters!

Read about two monsters. «Blip is green. It's got three eyes, four arms and two long antennae. It hasn't got any hair. It's got sharp teeth, but it's very friendly!» «Zuzu is purple. It's got one big eye, two short legs and a long tail. It hasn't got any arms.»

Answer: Has Blip got any hair? How many eyes has Zuzu got? En castellano: para animales y cosas usamos it, por eso es it's got.

12. Possessions: my favourite things

We also use have got for our possessions (things we own): toys, clothes, school things. «I've got a skateboard, a tablet and lots of books.» «My best friend has got a big collection of stickers.»

Use a before a consonant sound (a ball, a kite) and an before a vowel sound (an apple, an umbrella, an orange T-shirt). For plurals, use a number or some: «I've got three balls», «She's got some crayons».

13. One foot, two feet

Most English nouns make the plural with -s: one eye, two eyes; one arm, two arms. But some nouns are irregular: they change completely.

  • one foot → two feet (pie, pies)
  • one tooth → two teeth (diente, dientes)
  • one child → two children (niño, niños)
  • one man → two men; one woman → two women
  • one mouse → two mice (ratón, ratones)
  • one person → two people (persona, personas)
  • one fish → two fish (no change!)
  • one sheep → two sheep (no change!)

Some plurals add -es: one box, two boxes; one watch, two watches; one bus, two buses.

And words ending in consonant + y change to -ies: one baby, two babies; one puppy, two puppies.

These irregular plurals are very common when we describe people and animals: «The monster has got three feet and a hundred teeth!» «There are twenty children in my class.»

Activity: draw a funny monster and write how many feet, teeth and eyes it has got.

14. Let's practise: draw a monster

Play Monster dictation in pairs. Draw a secret monster. Don't show it! Describe it to your partner: «My monster has got two heads. It's got four eyes on each head. It hasn't got any legs, but it's got wings.» Your partner draws it.

Then compare the drawings. Are they similar? Now swap. Your partner can ask questions: «Has it got a tail?» — «Yes, it has. A long blue tail.» ¡Gana la pareja cuyo dibujo se parezca más!

15. Game: Guess who?

Guess who? (¿Quién es quién?) is a great game to practise have got and descriptions.

How to play:

  • 1. Each player has got a board with lots of faces. Every face is different: long or short hair, glasses, hats, beards…
  • 2. Each player chooses a secret person.
  • 3. Players take turns to ask yes/no questions: «Has your person got glasses?» «Is your person a man?» «Has she got curly hair?»
  • 4. The other player answers with short answers: «Yes, she has.» / «No, he hasn't.» / «Yes, he is.»
  • 5. Close the faces that are not possible.
  • 6. When you know, say: «Is it Anna?» The first player to find the secret person wins.

You can also play with your classmates. One pupil thinks of a classmate, and the others ask: «Has he got brown eyes? Is he tall? Has he got a blue jumper?»

Remember the short answers:

  • «Has he got…?» – «Yes, he has.» / «No, he hasn't.»
  • «Is she…?» – «Yes, she is.» / «No, she isn't.»

Activity: make your own Guess who? cards with drawings of eight people.

Lo hacemos juntos

Completa: «My brother ___ got a guitar.»

  1. My brother = he.
  2. Con he se usa has.

Resultado: My brother has got a guitar.

Pregunta si tu amiga tiene hermanos.

  1. Para preguntar, have delante.
  2. You → have.

Resultado: Have you got any brothers or sisters?

Corrige: «She has got eyes blue.»

  1. El adjetivo va delante del nombre.
  2. eyes blue → blue eyes.

Resultado: She's got blue eyes.

Write the short form: «She has got a red bike».

  1. She has = she's.
  2. Got stays after the short form.

Resultado: She's got a red bike.

Correct: «I haven't got brothers».

  1. Negative sentence with a plural.
  2. We need any before the noun.

Resultado: I haven't got any brothers.

Errores típicos

  • Usar have con he o she: «He have got» → «He has got».
  • Decir la edad con have: «I have got eight years» → «I'm eight».
  • Contestar con got: «Yes, I have got» → «Yes, I have».
  • Poner el color detrás: «hair black» → «black hair».
  • Decir «hairs» para el pelo de la cabeza: «He's got short hair».
  • Saying «Her hairs are long» instead of «Her hair is long».
  • Saying «two foots» or «three tooths» instead of «two feet» and «three teeth».

PracticaResponde sin mirar arriba. Equivocarse aquí también enseña.

Ejercicios (24)

Hazlos en tu cuaderno y después abre la solución.

Nivel básico

  1. Completa: «I ___ got a cat.»

    Ver solución
    have (I've got).

  2. Completa: «She ___ got curly hair.»

    Ver solución
    has (she's got).

  3. Escribe en negativa: «We've got a garden.»

    Ver solución
    We haven't got a garden.

  4. Write the short form of «they have got».

    Ver solución
    They've got.

  5. Complete: «I've got ___ orange».

    Ver solución
    An.

  6. How do you say «gafas» in English?

    Ver solución
    Glasses.

  7. What's the plural of «foot»?

    Ver solución
    Feet.

  8. In the reading, what's the name of the dog?

    Ver solución
    Biscuit.

Nivel medio

  1. Escribe en negativa: «He's got a bike.»

    Ver solución
    He hasn't got a bike.

  2. Pregunta: «they / a dog»

    Ver solución
    Have they got a dog?

  3. Respuesta corta: «Has your mum got a car?» (no)

    Ver solución
    No, she hasn't.

  4. Traduce: pelo rizado, ojos verdes.

    Ver solución
    curly hair, green eyes.

  5. ¿Cuál es el plural de foot y de tooth?

    Ver solución
    feet y teeth.

  6. Make a question: you / any pets.

    Ver solución
    Have you got any pets?

  7. Answer: Has a bird got fur?

    Ver solución
    No, it hasn't. It's got feathers.

  8. Order the words: hair / long / brown / she's got.

    Ver solución
    She's got long brown hair.

  9. Write the plural of child, mouse and person.

    Ver solución
    Children, mice, people.

  10. Describe Mrs Brown from the reading.

    Ver solución
    She's got grey hair and glasses.

Nivel avanzado

  1. ¿A o an? «___ umbrella», «___ kite».

    Ver solución
    an umbrella, a kite.

  2. Describe a un compañero con dos frases.

    Ver solución
    Model answer: Marta has got long brown hair. She's got brown eyes.

  3. Write a «Lost pet» poster with six sentences.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

  4. Write an animal riddle with has got.

    Ver solución
    Example: It's got a long neck and four legs. It's yellow and brown. It's a giraffe.

  5. Explain the two meanings of «He's» in «He's got a dog» and «He's eight».

    Ver solución
    He has got a dog; he is eight.

  6. Play Guess who? and write five questions you asked.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

Explícalo con tus palabrasComo si se lo contaras a alguien de un curso menor

¿Has nombrado estas ideas?
★

Situación de aprendizajeLost and found

The class makes «Lost» posters for imaginary pets and people, and plays a game to find them with descriptions.

Pasos

  1. Invent and draw a lost pet or a lost toy.
  2. Write a poster with be and have got.
  3. Read the posters and ask questions with «Has it got…?».
  4. Play Guess who? with drawings of the class.

Producto final: A wall of «Lost» posters and a class Guess who? game.

Cómo se valora

  • Uses have got and has got correctly.
  • Uses short forms and short answers.
  • Describes people and animals in detail.
  • Uses irregular plurals.

Tarjetas de repasoToca la tarjeta para darle la vuelta

Según cómo respondas, la tarjeta vuelve mañana, en 3, en 7 o en 21 días.

Para familias

  • Jugad a «¿Quién es quién?» en inglés: «Has he got glasses?», «Has she got long hair?».
  • Dibujad un monstruo a partir de una descripción en inglés y comparad el resultado.
  • Repasad juntos las tarjetas del paso 6 dos minutos al día durante una semana.

Para profesores

Saberes: Have got / has got en afirmativa, negativa e interrogativa, respuestas cortas, descripción física y partes del cuerpo (Lengua Extranjera: Inglés) (RD 157/2022, segundo ciclo de Primaria, 3.er curso).

  • Dictado de monstruos por parejas.
  • Juego de adivinar personajes con preguntas de sí o no.
  • Mural de la clase con descripciones físicas.

Revisado el 22 de noviembre de 2026.

Qué vas a aprender

  • Use have got and has got to talk about possessions and appearance
  • Make negative sentences with haven't got and hasn't got
  • Ask questions with Have you got…? / Has she got…? and give short answers
  • Describe people and monsters: hair, eyes and body parts
  • Use the short forms I've got and she's got
  • Use a, an and any with have got
  • Describe people and animals in detail
  • Use irregular plurals: feet, teeth, children

Palabras clave

have got · has got · haven't got · hasn't got · Have you got…? · Yes, I have · No, he hasn't · hair · eyes · body

Tiempo

80 minutos hoy + 2 minutos en cada repaso
